The environment-signals blueprint and the `mngr start` slowness investigation are updated to record the sleep/wake follow-up: the forward's cached SSH transports are now invalidated after a wake (without the minds-to-forward nudge channel the blueprint assumed), and the suspension watchdog covers the blocked-`mngr start` mechanism the investigation found.

`scripts/sleep_wake_probe.py` measures, across a real laptop sleep against a real SSH host, the platform facts that work relies on: that `time.monotonic()` stops during a sleep, which Python deadlines freeze with the machine, whether a blocked SSH read is released and by what, whether the watchdog's `transport.close()` releases one, how long a cached idle connection stalls on its first channel open after the wake, and how soon the host is reachable again. It reads the peer sshd's `ClientAliveInterval` from the keepalives it actually sends rather than from `sshd -T`, which is blind to the `-o` flags mngr passes on sshd's command line. `--black-hole` (macOS, sudo) reproduces the dead-NAT case, where packets on the old connections vanish without a reply, with a pf rule scoped to the probe's own local ports.

`scripts/sleep_wake_drill.py` is the companion that exercises the assembled system rather than the substrate. `uv run --script scripts/sleep_wake_drill.py --auto-sleep` is the whole invocation: it finds every running minds backend in the process table, takes each one's log file, data directory and mngr from that app's own argv, and reports what each app did against the one sleep they share. A laptop running a build under test beside a build from main is therefore drilled as one run, on one outage and one sleep; two separate runs could not answer the same question, since they would be two different networks and two different sleeps. `--dry-run` resolves every app and machine and checks each is reachable without installing a rule or sleeping the laptop.

It stages two scenarios, because a sleep does two different things to minds. `--scenario post-wake-tunnel` (the default) is the incident the branch is named for: nothing is staged before the sleep, so both apps go under with healthy machines and healthy tunnels, and at the wake every connection open to the machines is killed by its local port and nothing else is. That is what the incident's network did -- the NAT had dropped the mappings for the connections that predated the sleep, so packets on them vanished without a reply, while a fresh connection to the same address went straight through -- and the machines answer throughout, so a machine called stuck was called stuck wrongly and an unattended start dispatched for it restarted a machine that was running, which is why, in that scenario, convicting is the failure the report names. Blocking the whole address instead stages a machine that is unreachable for as long as the block lasts, which both builds are right to convict and which cannot tell a tunnel rebuilt before use from one handed back half-open; two runs staged that way before this was understood, and read as both builds failing. The connections are read off the kernel at the first gap and the rule goes in then rather than at the settled wake, since the app's first request after a wake reaches the forward within seconds and it is that request hanging, rather than being refused, that produces the failure run under test; the rule then stays in for the rest of the run, as the incident's connections never came back either. Because a fresh connect goes through by design, the rule is proven from a local port the drill holds and names beside the killed ones: a connect from it has to hang, a connect from a fresh port has to answer, and the release is confirmed the same way. The report reads whether the outage was real off those checks rather than off the app's log, since a build that retires its tunnels at the wake never sends a byte on a dead connection and logs no failure at all. `--scenario recovery-across-sleep` is the other half: the machines are taken off the network first, the apps are left to convict them and dispatch restarts, and the laptop sleeps across those restarts, so what is under test is what the sleep does to a `mngr start` whose every deadline is measured on a clock the sleep stops.

Root is taken once, at the start, and held by a helper process for the length of the run. Nothing in a run that sleeps the laptop can rely on sudo's credential cache: it lasts five minutes, a refresher thread is frozen while the machine is suspended, and the one `pfctl` that matters runs on the far side of the sleep. One run lost twenty-six minutes to exactly that -- the drill blocked on a password prompt nobody was there to answer, the laptop idled back to sleep behind it, and the post-wake window it went on to measure was one in which the network had never come back. The helper also owns the rule's lifetime and lifts it on a deadman, so a run that crashes, is interrupted or is killed cannot leave the laptop unable to reach the workspaces, and every removal is confirmed by reconnecting rather than by `pfctl`'s exit code: a removal reported but not made is the one failure that stops anyone looking.

Two preconditions the drill states up front, because without either an app's column measures nothing: the app must be running the code you meant to test, and a window must stay open on its workspace, since the health probe loop only polls agents that a failed request has enrolled as suspect and those requests come from a page loading the workspace. The outage stays scoped to the workspace addresses rather than cutting the whole network, and that is not a convenience: minds withholds an unattended start when it reads the device itself as offline -- the reading is whether any of github.com, gitlab.com or bitbucket.org answers on 443 -- and records the start as merely owed, so a blanket block would leave nothing in flight for the sleep to land in and would measure the offline path instead of this one. Each app's mngr is the one beside the `minds` it is running, which is its own for an installed app and the checkout's for a dev app; the drill runs it from the home directory, as the app does, since mngr layers in the project config of whatever directory it is run from and a checkout's `.mngr/settings.toml` declares providers whose backends an app-bundled mngr does not ship. It reads the entry point from anywhere in the argv rather than the front, since a console script is exec'd through its interpreter, and requires it to be a path, since the launcher process above each backend carries the same `run` and the same `--log-file` and would otherwise enter the run as a second app. The drill proves the outage it stages: every app's endpoint must accept a TCP connect before the block goes in and refuse one under it, so a run where an app never reacted cannot be confused with a run where nothing was ever blocked for it. It refuses to target an agent discovery did not name, and never offers one among the choices for an ambiguous query -- those cannot be told apart from each other or from the system-services agent, which is the agent a recovery acts on rather than one a recovery is staged for. Both scripts also ask for the sudo password up front and hold the credential open for the run, since a run lasts well past sudo's five-minute cache and neither installing nor lifting a block can wait on a prompt nobody is there to answer.

On battery, expect several sleep gaps rather than one: macOS dark-wakes partway through a sleep, each of which ends the interval as far as the app is concerned, re-arming its post-wake grace and re-marking the in-flight start. The drill waits for the machine to stay awake past `--wake-settle` before treating a gap as the wake, so it does not lift the block during a dark wake, and the report says how many gaps there were. It also holds an idle-sleep assertion (`caffeinate -i`) for the run: a laptop whose display has gone dark idles back to sleep a couple of minutes after the wake, and one run re-slept three times that way, each time restarting the countdowns and moving the wake the report was timed from. The assertion is against idle sleep only, so the sleep the run asks for with `pmset sleepnow` goes ahead.
